cues.text: Here's a paper that shaped a lot of the AI agents you use today.
It's called ReAct: short for Reason, plus Act.
Picture yourself cooking.
You think: everything is chopped, so now I boil the water.
You hit a problem: no salt, so you grab soy sauce instead.
And when you're stuck, you act. You open a recipe and look it up.
In twenty twenty-two, language models did one or the other.
Chain-of-thought models reasoned, but only from memory, so they could confidently invent facts.
Acting models searched and clicked, but never stopped to think about the goal.
ReAct simply lets the model do both, in turns.
It writes a thought,
takes an action,
reads what the world sends back,
and thinks again, until it can answer.
The result? On a household game, it beat specially trained agents by thirty-four points.
On a shopping website, by ten points.
And it learned from only one or two examples.
So remember this: reasoning guides action,
and action keeps reasoning honest.
Let's see how it works.
Let's open the hood. It's simpler than you'd think.
Think of an agent, talking to an environment, like Wikipedia or a game.
At each step, it sends an action, and gets an observation back.
The trouble is: picking the right action sometimes needs real thinking, and there's nowhere to do it.
ReAct's fix is one line.
Take the usual set of actions, and add all of language to it.
A thought becomes just another action, but one that doesn't touch the world.
It's only written into the model's context, like a note to self.
Thoughts can do many jobs.
They break a goal into a plan,
bring in common sense,
recover when a search fails,
and keep track of progress.
And there's no training at all.
A frozen model sees a few examples written by humans, and continues the pattern.
For questions, it thinks at every step.
For long tasks, it decides for itself when a thought is worth it.
Let's replay the paper's favourite example.
The question: aside from the Apple Remote, what other device can control the program it was designed for?
It needs two hops: find the program, then find what else controls it.
Chain-of-thought answers from memory.
It assumes the remote was made for Apple TV. That's false, and every step after inherits the mistake.
Acting alone does find the right pages.
But with no thinking in between, it can't pull out the answer, and finishes with: yes.
ReAct plans first, then searches.
When a search fails, a thought fixes the query.
And the last thought pulls out the answer: keyboard function keys. Correct.
Thoughts aim the actions.
Observations correct the thoughts. That's the whole trick.
Now, the numbers. First: question answering, and fact checking.
The model gets a deliberately weak Wikipedia tool, with three actions.
Search for a page,
look up a word, like control F,
and finish with an answer.
Here's a surprise. On HotpotQA, ReAct alone is slightly behind chain-of-thought.
On FEVER, it's ahead.
And the best scores of all come from combining the two.
Why? Because they fail in different ways.
More than half of chain-of-thought's failures are made-up facts.
For ReAct, that number is zero. Its weak spot is getting stuck, repeating itself, or chasing a useless search.
So the authors combine them.
Ask chain-of-thought many times.
If most answers agree, trust them.
If they don't, the model's memory is shaky, so switch to ReAct and go look it up.
One more twist. Fine-tune on just three thousand ReAct examples,
and it becomes the best method. A small fine-tuned model beats every prompted method on a model almost eight times bigger.
Next, tasks where the model has to act for a long time.
ALFWorld is a text game set in a house. Find a pepper shaker, put it in a drawer.
WebShop is a shopping website, with over a million real products.
Here, thoughts are sparse.
One thought makes a plan from common sense: pepper shakers are usually in cabinets, or on countertops.
Another marks progress, and picks the next goal.
The result: seventy-one percent success, against forty-five for acting alone,
and thirty-seven for an agent trained on a hundred thousand examples per task type.
On WebShop, ReAct jumps ten points above the previous best.
Humans are still far ahead, though.
And just describing the room isn't enough.
When thoughts only narrate the environment, success drops to fifty-three. Real reasoning is what helps.
Finally, the parts that don't fit in a table.
Because thoughts are plain text, a human can edit them.
Delete one wrong sentence, add a hint, and the agent finishes the task.
Two edits, instead of dozens of actions.
Acting also keeps answers fresh.
In one question, the dataset's answer was out of date.
Only ReAct searched,
and found the current one. The benchmark marked it wrong anyway.
There are limits.
Prompts can only hold so many examples.
Fully trained systems still score higher on question answering.
And an agent that can act can also do harm, so the authors kept it in safe sandboxes.
The whole paper fits in one line: let models think, and act, in turns.
You'll recognise that loop in many of the AI agents built since.
